title: Backend Trading System
summary: Receive trading requests through a simple API.
Persist reliable state as the source of truth.
Process background work asynchronously and safely.

sections.title: High-Level Approach
points: Keep synchronous work minimal.
Persist state before background processing.
Process asynchronous work with reliable workers.
speakingNotes: I would keep the API simple and make the write durable.
The database stores the important state before work continues.

sections.title: Architecture
points: The API validates incoming requests.
PostgreSQL stores the durable system state.
Kafka carries events for asynchronous processing.
Workers process jobs independently and can scale horizontally.
speakingNotes: The request first reaches the API for validation.
Then I persist the important state in PostgreSQL.
Kafka separates the request path from background processing.
sections.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Client --> API
  API --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]
  API --> Kafka
  Kafka --> Worker

sections.title: Data Flow
points: Validate the request and authenticate the caller.
Persist the request and its initial state.
Publish an event after the state is durable.
Let a worker process the event and update status.
speakingNotes: I will walk through one request from the client inward.
First I validate the input and persist the initial state.
The worker can retry without losing the original request.

sections.title: Key Decisions
points: PostgreSQL is the source of truth.
Workers must be idempotent.
Events need retries and dead-letter handling.
The API stays stateless for straightforward scaling.
speakingNotes: The key decision is to optimise for durable state.
Idempotency makes retries safe when a worker fails.
A dead-letter path prevents one bad event blocking the queue.

sections.title: Risks
points: Duplicate events can trigger repeated work.
Worker failures can leave requests in progress.
Database failures can affect both reads and writes.
Operational visibility is needed for stuck jobs.
speakingNotes: Failures are expected in production, so retries must be safe.
I would monitor queue depth, latency, and failed attempts.
The system should expose enough state to investigate incidents.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: Use a simple synchronous API at the edge.
Keep durable state in a reliable database.
Move slow work to retryable asynchronous workers.
Scale each part independently as demand grows.
speakingNotes: Overall I would optimise for reliability and clear ownership.
The design can start small and scale each component gradually.
That keeps the first version easy to operate and explain.
